title: Emrys and the Bridge
premise: In a war-shadowed river city, Ulyana Yarrow, apprentice to the late mapmaker Emrys, secretly completes the atlas he died protecting—a survey of bridges, fords, and hidden crossings that could decide the occupation's fate. When an unknown woman leaves a child at their door with orders to forget her face, Ulyana realizes the girl carries proof of what happened at the eastern bridge, evidence the occupiers will kill to bury. To survive, Ulyana must choose between the invisibility that kept them alive and the belonging they never dared want, smuggling both child and atlas past three checkpoints as the net tightens. In the end, Ulyana delivers the evidence across the water at terrible cost—burning their own name from every record—and finds that identity, once surrendered, can be redrawn like any map.
about_author: Ulyana Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing displaced-persons records from occupied Europe. She writes historical fiction about the quiet people history forgets to count.

chapters.title: The Weight of Rivers
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Working alone in Emrys's cold workshop, Ulyana inks the final plates of his atlas by candlelight, measuring distances in what can be carried if they must flee. The emotional beat is grief braided with discipline: the atlas is both inheritance and death warrant.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. On the eve of the atlas's completion, a woman leaves a mute girl, Mira, on the doorstep with a note: forget this face. Inside the child's coat lining, Ulyana finds a photograph of soldiers at the eastern bridge—the bridge Emrys mapped last. Fear replaces grief; invisibility is no longer possible.

chapters.title: What the Master Knew
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, with flashback fragments of Emrys. Searching his hidden papers, Ulyana deciphers marginalia proving the bridge was destroyed deliberately, not collapsed—massacre disguised as accident. The beat is horrified understanding: finishing the atlas means becoming its witness.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Count Windows
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The block warden begins noting visitors; a sympathetic neighbor, Halina, warns that informants have marked the workshop. Ulyana must decide whether to trust anyone. Emotional beat: the ache of isolation versus the risk of belonging, embodied in Halina's offered hand.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Planning the route south, Ulyana studies their own maps like battle plans: the fish-market checkpoint, the rail yard, the pontoon bridge. Mira begins to speak, revealing fragments of the bridge night. Beat: resolve hardening into purpose; the mapmaker becomes the smuggler.

chapters.title: The Fish Market
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. First checkpoint: Ulyana hides atlas plates beneath salted herring barrels while Mira plays the deaf-mute. A soldier recognizes something in Ulyana's face—an old classmate now in uniform. Beat: terror laced with strange mercy; he lets them pass but takes Ulyana's papers as 'verification,' a leash.

chapters.title: Halina's Betrayal or Gift
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Halina reveals she informed—not out of malice, but because the occupiers hold her son, and she traded the workshop's location for his life. She gives Ulyana her own travel pass instead. Beat: fury dissolving into forgiveness; the price of survival paid by everyone.

chapters.title: The Rail Yard
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Second checkpoint goes wrong: a random search separates Ulyana from Mira, who is loaded toward a transit train. Ulyana must abandon the atlas satchel to claw her back. Beat: the climax of sacrifice—choosing the child over the master's life work, then discovering Mira had sewn the key plate into her dress all along.

chapters.title: The Pontoon Bridge
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Climax. At the third checkpoint, the classmate-soldier waits, ordered to detain them. Ulyana gives him not pleas but the truth—the photograph, the massacre—and watches him break. He waves them across as sirens rise behind. Beat: catharsis; one man's conscience tips the scale.

chapters.title: Redrawn
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, epilogue tone. Across the border, Ulyana hands the atlas and photograph to Allied officers, then burns their old identity papers and draws a new map—one road, two travelers, no borders. Final beat: belonging found not in a place but in a person; identity as something made, not given.
